page.title: sus.bot | robots.txt checker
page.description: Free robots.txt checker. Fetch any site's robots.txt, see which search engines and AI crawlers are allowed or blocked, test paths against the rules, and check how the server responds to each crawler.
page.h1: Check and understand your robots.txt before traffic drops
page.intro: Enter your domain above. You get a verdict for the business, a fix list that links to the exact lines, and a message you can send straight to IT.
page.urlLabel: Domain, or any address on the site
page.urlHint: Paste whatever you have: a domain, a page, a link from an email, even the robots.txt address itself. We read /robots.txt from that site and ignore the rest.
page.agentsIntro: Resolved per crawler with RFC 9309 matching: the most specific group wins, then the longest rule, and ties go to Allow.
page.accessIntro: Request the file again through the proxy, identifying as each crawler in turn. A different status or body means the server treats that crawler differently (bot blocking, WAF rules, cloaking).
page.securityIntro: Disallow rules that name sensitive files and folders, which attackers look for first. This checks what the file reveals, not whether the paths exist or are protected.
page.reconIntro: What a stranger learns about this site from the file alone: the platform it runs on, cloud buckets, other hostnames, API entry points, data feeds, file types, and notes left in comments. Nothing here is fetched or probed; it is read straight from the text.
page.footerRfc: Rule matching follows RFC 9309 and Google's published crawler behaviour.
page.footerBy: A free tool by Sitefig.
page.noscript: This tool runs entirely in your browser and needs JavaScript.
parser.tooLarge: Crawlers stop reading this file after the first 500 KiB, so every rule after that point is ignored. The file is {kib} KiB.
parser.bom: A crawler with a strict parser may misread the first line, because the file starts with a UTF-8 byte-order mark. Save the file without one.
parser.notFieldValue: Crawlers ignore this line, because it is not written as "directive: value".
parser.misspelling: Crawlers other than Google may skip this line, because "{raw}" is a misspelling of "{field}". Google reads it as "{field}".
parser.emptyUserAgent: The rules under this line apply to no crawler, because the User-agent line names none.
parser.emptyUserAgent.others: This line adds no crawler to the group, because the User-agent value is empty. The rules under it apply to {names}.
parser.emptyUserAgent.star: This line adds no crawler to the group, because the User-agent value is empty. The rules under it apply to every crawler without its own rules.
parser.invalidToken: The rules under this line apply to no crawler, because "{value}" is not a valid crawler name.
parser.invalidToken.others: This line adds no crawler to the group, because "{value}" is not a valid crawler name. The rules under it apply to {names}.
parser.invalidToken.star: This line adds no crawler to the group, because "{value}" is not a valid crawler name. The rules under it apply to every crawler without its own rules.
parser.tokenTail: These rules apply to "{token}", not to "{value}". Crawlers read only the name and ignore what follows it.
parser.ruleBeforeAgent: Crawlers ignore this {directive} line, because it comes before any User-agent line.
parser.ruleBeforeAgent.disallow: {outcome} This line was meant to block it, but it comes before any User-agent line, so crawlers ignore it.
parser.ruleBeforeAgent.allow: {outcome} This line was meant to open it, but it comes before any User-agent line, so crawlers ignore it.
parser.emptyAllow: This line changes nothing, because an Allow without a path matches no URL.
parser.emptyDisallow: This line blocks nothing, because a Disallow without a path leaves every URL open.
parser.pathNoSlash.disallow: {outcome} This line was meant to block it, but "{value}" does not start with "/", so it matches no URL. Write "/{value}".
parser.pathNoSlash.allow: {outcome} This line was meant to open it, but "{value}" does not start with "/", so it matches no URL. Write "/{value}".
parser.crawlDelayBeforeAgent: No crawler slows down for this Crawl-delay line, because it comes before any User-agent line and is ignored.
parser.crawlDelayNaN: No crawler slows down for this line, because "{value}" is not a number.
parser.crawlDelayDuplicate: Crawlers ignore this Crawl-delay, because the group already has one and the first one is kept.
parser.crawlDelayNonStandard: Only Bing slows down for Crawl-delay. Google and Yandex ignore it, because it is not part of RFC 9309.
parser.sitemapInvalid: Crawlers cannot find this sitemap, because "{value}" is not a full address that starts with http:// or https://.
parser.hostDuplicate: This Host line is ignored, because the file already has one and the first one is kept.
parser.hostObsolete: No crawler reads this Host line. Host was a Yandex-only directive for naming the main mirror, and Yandex dropped it in 2018. Redirect to the preferred hostname instead.
parser.cleanParamMalformed: Yandex ignores this Clean-param line, because it is malformed. Write "Clean-param: p1&p2 /path-prefix", with parameter names made of letters, digits, "_", "-" and ".".
parser.cleanParamTooLong: Yandex ignores this Clean-param line, because it is longer than the {max} characters Yandex accepts.
parser.cleanParamInfo: Only Yandex follows this line: it leaves out the listed query parameters when it crawls. Every other crawler ignores Clean-param.
parser.noindex: This line keeps no page out of search results, because no major search engine supports Noindex in robots.txt. Use a robots meta tag or the X-Robots-Tag header instead.
parser.unknownDirective: Crawlers ignore this line, because "{field}" is not a directive they know.
parser.noRules: Every crawler may read every page, because the file holds no rules.
parser.emptyGroup: The crawlers this group names may read every page, because the group has no rules.
parser.emptyGroup.merged: This group adds no rules. The crawlers it names follow the rules of their other groups in this file.
parser.tokenRepeated: Older crawlers may follow only part of the rules for "{token}", because the name appears in {n} groups. RFC 9309 merges the groups, but older crawlers may use only the first.
parser.starBlocksAll: The whole site is blocked for every crawler without its own group, because the "*" group disallows it.
parser.noSitemap: Crawlers have to find new pages by following links, because the file lists no sitemap. A Sitemap line is optional, but it helps them.
seo.trailingSlash.allow: URLs such as {path}s, {path}-old and {path}2 are open too, because "{path}" is a prefix and matches every URL that starts with it. Write "{path}/" for the directory, or "{path}$" for only that URL.
seo.trailingSlash.disallow: URLs such as {path}s, {path}-old and {path}2 are blocked too, because "{path}" is a prefix and matches every URL that starts with it. Write "{path}/" for the directory, or "{path}$" for only that URL.
seo.selfBlock: Crawlers other than Google may stop reading your rules altogether, because "Disallow: {path}" also matches /robots.txt. Google fetches robots.txt regardless.
seo.caseSensitive: {outcome} This line covers only URLs written exactly as "{path}", because paths are case-sensitive. Check the casing of the site's real URLs.
seo.duplicate: This line changes nothing, because "{rule}" repeats line {line}{scope}.
seo.redundant: This line changes nothing, because every URL "{rule}" matches is already covered by "{winner}" on line {line}{scope}.
seo.overridden.disallow: {path} stays open, because "{winner}" on line {line} wins over "{rule}" on every URL it matches{scope}.
seo.overridden.allow: {path} stays blocked, because "{winner}" on line {line} wins over "{rule}" on every URL it matches{scope}.
outcome.open.default: {path} is open to every crawler without its own rules in this file.
outcome.allowed.all: {path} is open to every crawler, because "{winner}" on line {line} allows it.
outcome.allowed.default: {path} is open to every crawler without its own rules in this file, because "{winner}" on line {line} allows it.
outcome.allowed.named: {path} is open to {names}, because "{winner}" on line {line} allows it.
outcome.blocked.all: {path} is blocked for every crawler, by "{winner}" on line {line}.
outcome.blocked.default: {path} is blocked for every crawler without its own rules in this file, by "{winner}" on line {line}.
outcome.blocked.named: {path} is blocked for {names}, by "{winner}" on line {line}.
sitemap.duplicate: This line adds nothing, because the same sitemap is already listed on line {line}.
sitemap.protocolMismatch: Crawlers hit a redirect or an insecure copy every time they fetch this sitemap, because the site is served over https and the sitemap is listed as http. Use {url}.
sitemap.httpsOnHttp: Crawlers fetch this sitemap over https, while the site was reached over http. This is fine if the site redirects to https; otherwise list the sitemap with the protocol the site uses.
sitemap.crossDomain: Search engines may ignore this sitemap, because it is hosted on {host} and not on {site}. Google accepts it only when both sites are verified by the same owner in Search Console (cross-site submission).
sitemap.otherSubdomain: Crawlers accept this sitemap. It sits on another host of the same domain ({host}), and listing it here is what allows it to contain {site} URLs.
lint.absoluteUrl: "{rule}" matches no URL, because a rule must be a path and this is a full address. The line also publishes the hostname.
lint.absoluteUrl.disallow: {outcome} This line was meant to block it, but "{rule}" is a full address and a rule must be a path, so it matches no URL. Write "{path}". The line also publishes the hostname.
lint.absoluteUrl.allow: {outcome} This line was meant to open it, but "{rule}" is a full address and a rule must be a path, so it matches no URL. Write "{path}". The line also publishes the hostname.
fetch.warn.redirectLimit: Google treats this site as having no robots.txt, so no page is restricted. The file sits behind more than five redirects, and RFC 9309 lets crawlers give up at that point.
fetch.warn.redirectSameSite: Crawlers still reach the file. robots.txt redirects to {host}, and crawlers follow a www or https redirect like this one.
fetch.warn.redirectOtherHost: {from} is governed by the rules of {to}, because robots.txt redirects to that host and crawlers apply the file they land on.
fetch.warn.notRobotsPath: Crawlers read the content of {path} as your robots.txt, because the redirect ended there and not at /robots.txt.
fetch.error.unsupportedProtocol: Only http and https URLs are supported.
fetch.error.notHostname: "{host}" does not look like a hostname.
fetch.error.cors: Direct fetch was blocked. The site does not send CORS headers for robots.txt.
fetch.error.noProxy: The proxy is not configured. Set WORKER_URL in js/config.js.
fetch.error.proxyTimeout: The proxy did not answer in time.
fetch.error.proxyUnreadable: The proxy returned an unreadable response (HTTP {status}).
fetch.error.rateLimited: Too many requests: the proxy is rate-limited right now. Wait a minute and try again.
fetch.error.paused: The proxy is switched off at the moment, so only sites that send CORS headers can be fetched. Paste the robots.txt instead.
fetch.error.originRefused: The proxy refused this page's origin. Add it to ALLOWED_ORIGINS in worker/wrangler.toml.
fetch.error.noProxyFallback: {reason} No proxy is configured, so the file cannot be read. Paste its contents instead.
security.reconWarning: Attackers read the Disallow lines of this file to decide where to look first, because robots.txt is public and is not access control. Protect every path listed here with authentication, remove it from the web root, or mark it noindex with an HTTP header.
security.category.admin.label: Admin / internal
security.category.admin.advice: Protect with authentication and send an X-Robots-Tag: noindex header. Listing it here only advertises where the login is.
security.category.staging.label: Staging / dev
security.category.staging.advice: Take staging and test environments off the public internet, or restrict them by IP or login. Use a noindex header rather than robots.txt.
security.category.backups.label: Backups & archives
security.category.backups.advice: Backups and archives should not be reachable over HTTP at all. Move them outside the web root and verify the URL returns 404.
security.category.secrets.label: Secrets & config
security.category.secrets.advice: Configuration files, version-control folders and credentials must never be web-accessible. Block them at the server and check they return 403 or 404.
security.category.api.label: Private APIs & debug
security.category.api.advice: Internal APIs and debug endpoints need authentication or a network allowlist. Crawlers are not the threat here; scripted scanners are.
security.category.data.label: User data & uploads
security.category.data.advice: Turn off directory listing and make sure private files require a login. A Disallow only asks polite crawlers to look away.
security.reason.versioned: Versioned path, often an old or unreleased version
security.reason.configFile: Configuration, version control or credential file

md.glance.noStar: No `*` group, so everything is allowed
md.glance.default: **Default policy** for crawlers without their own group: {policy}
md.issues.plusNotes: Plus {notes}, listed in the full report.
md.security.none: No Disallow rule points at a commonly sensitive location.
md.security.intro: Disallow lines are public and are routinely scanned for reconnaissance. robots.txt is not access control; anything below needs authentication, removal from the web root, or a noindex header instead.
md.security.plusLow: Plus {findings} (uploads, user data) in the full report.
md.recon.envPaths: **Paths that look like another environment or redesign:** {list}
md.recon.nothing: Nothing notable. The file reveals little beyond its rules.
md.sitemaps.none: No Sitemap line. Optional, but it helps crawlers discover URLs.
md.actions.redirectChain: Fix the redirect chain on /robots.txt: crawlers give up after five hops and treat the file as missing.
md.actions.serverError: Fix the server error on /robots.txt. Google treats 5xx as "disallow everything" for up to 30 days.
md.actions.trailingSlash: Decide whether {rules} should end in "/" (directory) or "$" (exact URL); as written they also match longer paths{where}.
md.actions.selfBlock: Remove the rule that matches /robots.txt itself{where}.
md.actions.noSlash: Add the leading "/" to {paths} that can never match{where}.
md.actions.crossDomain: Verify cross-domain sitemap ownership in Search Console, or move {sitemaps} onto this domain{where}.
md.actions.addSitemap: Add a Sitemap line pointing at the XML sitemap.
md.actions.noindex: Move noindex out of robots.txt into a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header; no search engine honours it here.
md.actions.crawlDelay: Treat Crawl-delay as Bing-only; use Search Console crawl settings for Google.
md.actions.starBlocked: Confirm that blocking the whole site for every crawler without its own group is intended.
md.actions.aiUneven: Decide on one AI-training policy. Still allowed or only partly restricted: {list}.
md.actions.aiDecide: Decide whether AI training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot and others) should be allowed; none is restricted today.
md.actions.buckets: Check permissions on the cloud buckets named in the file: {list}.
md.actions.envHosts: Remove non-production hostnames from the file and put those environments behind authentication: {list}.
md.actions.personal: Strip names, email addresses, IPs and ticket IDs from comments; the file is public.
md.actions.bom: Save the file as UTF-8 without a byte-order mark.
md.actions.none: No action needed. The file is clean.
ui.status.viaProxy: Direct fetch blocked by CORS. Fetching through the proxy…
ui.status.example: Analysed example, checks assume the site is {url}
ui.status.pasteFirst: Paste the contents of a robots.txt first.
ui.summary.redirectLimit.title: The file sends crawlers in circles
ui.summary.redirectLimit.body: Too many redirects to follow, so Google gives up and treats your site as having no instructions at all. The chain needs shortening.
ui.summary.notFound.title: There is no robots.txt at all
ui.summary.notFound.body: Crawlers take a missing file as permission to read the whole site, AI crawlers included. If you want any say over that, the file has to exist.
ui.summary.clientError.body: The file could not be read, and crawlers take that as permission to read everything. Nothing you put in the file is being obeyed.
ui.summary.serverError.title: Your server is failing to hand the file over
ui.summary.serverError.body: Google reads this as "stay away from the whole site" for up to a month, and your pages start dropping out of search while it lasts. Whoever runs the server needs to know today.
ui.summary.unexpectedStatus.title: The file could not be read
ui.summary.unexpectedStatus.body: The server gave an answer crawlers will not accept, so the rules in the file are being ignored.
ui.summary.html.title: That is a web page, not a robots.txt
ui.summary.html.body: The server answered with a page instead of the file, usually a "not found" page dressed up. Crawlers find no instructions in it, so nothing you wrote is in force.
ui.summary.empty.title: The file is empty, so nothing is being asked
ui.summary.empty.body: An empty file means every crawler may read every page. If you expected it to block a crawler or a page, that instruction is not here.
ui.summary.noStar.title: No general instruction, so most crawlers do as they please
ui.summary.noStar.body: The file only speaks to the crawlers it names. Every other crawler, including most AI crawlers, reads that as permission to read the whole site.
ui.summary.allBlocked.title: Your whole site is closed to search engines
ui.summary.allBlocked.body: The file tells every crawler to stay out of everything. Google, Bing and the rest will drop the pages they already have. Only a crawler named separately further down gets in.
ui.summary.open.title: Everything is open to everyone
ui.summary.open.body: Nothing in this file holds any crawler back. That is fine if you meant it, and worth deciding if you did not: it includes the AI crawlers listed below.
ui.summary.restricted.title: Parts of your site are hidden
ui.summary.restricted.body: {disallow} rules keep pages out of search and {allow} rules let pages back in. Check below that the hidden pages are the ones you meant, and that no page you sell from is among them.
ui.export.audit.title: Client audit
ui.export.audit.note: An executive summary with recommended actions. Paste the Markdown into Notion, Google Docs or a ticket; the rich-text copy keeps headings and tables in email and Docs.
ui.export.sheet.title: Spreadsheet
ui.export.sheet.note: Four sheets: rules, sitemaps and HTTP status, warnings and traps, recon and asset leaks. Copy a sheet and paste straight into Google Sheets or Excel, or download CSV files.
ui.export.json.title: JSON for your tools
ui.export.json.note: The full analysis as one JSON document. It declares its schema, so dashboards and scripts can validate it: {link}.
ui.export.share.title: Share
ui.export.share.live: A link that re-runs this analysis live. The robots.txt is fetched again when opened, so results reflect the file at that time.
ui.export.share.noLive: Links can only re-run analyses of a fetched URL. Pasted text and examples have no live source to link to.
ui.ai.legend: Blocked means the whole site is disallowed for that crawler. Restricted means part of the site is disallowed. Hover a pill for details.

parser.utf16: Many crawlers will not find a single valid line in this file, because it is saved as UTF-16 and RFC 9309 requires UTF-8. Save the file as UTF-8.
parser.htmlFragment: Crawlers cannot read the lines with HTML markup ("{tag}"), and the markup can break the rule next to it. It usually comes from a theme, a plugin or a cache layer.
parser.pluginOutput: Crawlers meet lines they cannot read, because a caching or minification plugin has added its output to robots.txt. Exclude /robots.txt from that plugin.
parser.serverErrorOutput: robots.txt shows a server error message to every visitor, such as a PHP warning or a stack trace. It can reveal file paths on the server, and it breaks the rules around it.
parser.invalidUtf8: Part of this file is lost to crawlers, because it is not valid UTF-8 and the characters that cannot be decoded are dropped. RFC 9309 requires UTF-8.
parser.longLine: Crawlers may cut this line short and lose the end of the rule, because it is {chars} characters long. A line that long is generated, not written.
parser.gluedComment: Crawlers ignore this "{directive}" line, because a line break is missing before it and it has become part of a comment.
parser.gluedComment.disallow: {outcome} This line was meant to block it, but a line break is missing before "{directive}", so the rule has become part of a comment and crawlers ignore it.
parser.gluedComment.allow: {outcome} This line was meant to open it, but a line break is missing before "{directive}", so the rule has become part of a comment and crawlers ignore it.
lint.commentedRule: This line does nothing, because it is a "{directive}" rule that has been commented out.
parser.invisibleChar: Crawlers skip this line, because an invisible character sits in front of the directive name and they read the name as unknown. Retype the line.
parser.homoglyph: Crawlers skip this line, because "{field}" is written with a letter from another alphabet that only looks the same. Retype it in plain Latin letters.
parser.fullwidthColon: Crawlers skip this line, because it uses a full-width colon instead of ":". Crawlers only accept the plain colon.
parser.junkBeforeField: Crawlers ignore this "{field}" line, because "{junk}" sits before the directive name and they read it as part of the name. Remove what comes before the name.
parser.hashInValue: {outcome} This line was written as "{value}", but "#" starts a comment, so crawlers read the rule as "{truncated}". Remove the fragment; URL fragments are never sent to the server.
parser.hashInValue.sitemap: Crawlers read this sitemap address as "{truncated}", not "{value}", because "#" starts a comment and cuts the line short. Remove the fragment; URL fragments are never sent to the server.
parser.placeholder: This line may not apply to your site, because "{value}" still contains the template placeholder "{placeholder}". Replace it with your own value.
parser.crawlDelayHigh: Bing can crawl only about {pages} pages a day, because Crawl-delay is {seconds} seconds. A large site will not be crawled in full.
parser.wildcardOnly: Google reads this line as "block the whole site", while other crawlers read "{value}" as a literal path. "Disallow: {value}" is not RFC 9309. Write "Disallow: /" if you mean the whole site.
parser.spaceInPath: Crawlers may not match this rule, because "{value}" contains a space and URLs never contain raw spaces. Write %20, or split the rule in two.
parser.regexSyntax: This rule does not match the URLs it was written for, because "{value}" uses regular-expression syntax. robots.txt only understands "*" and "$", and every other character is matched literally.
parser.nonAsciiPath: Not every crawler matches this rule, because "{value}" contains non-ASCII characters. RFC 9309 matches percent-encoded paths; most crawlers encode the path for you, but not all.
parser.bareUrl: Crawlers ignore this line, because it holds only a URL. If this is your sitemap, write "Sitemap: {url}".
parser.metaRobots: Crawlers ignore this line, because "{field}" is a meta robots value and not a robots.txt directive. Use a meta robots tag or the X-Robots-Tag header instead.
parser.aiDirective: This line blocks no AI crawler that follows the standard, because "{field}" is a proposed extension and not part of RFC 9309. Name the AI crawlers you want to block in User-agent groups.
parser.nonStandardDirective: Crawlers ignore this line today. "{field}" is not part of RFC 9309, although crawlers once honoured it.
parser.contentSignal: Only crawlers that support Content-Signal follow this line, which states how the site may be used ({value}). It is Cloudflare's extension, not part of RFC 9309.
parser.contentSignalInvalid: Crawlers cannot read this Content-Signal line, because it is malformed at {parts}. Each entry is search, ai-input or ai-train, set to yes or no.
parser.notFieldValue.hint: Crawlers ignore this line, because the ":" between the directive and its value is missing. Did you mean "{field}"?
security.injectedCode: The site or one of its plugins may have been compromised for SEO spam, because robots.txt contains script, iframe or hidden-link markup. Check the server for malicious code.
seo.queryStringBlock: Paginated, filtered and tracked landing pages are blocked for every crawler without its own rules, because "Disallow: {path}" matches every URL with a query string.
seo.assetBlock: Every crawler without its own rules is cut off from the scripts or styles your pages need, because "Disallow: {path}" blocks them. A search engine that cannot load them cannot render the page the way visitors see it.
seo.cssJsBlock: Every crawler without its own rules is cut off from CSS or JavaScript files, because "Disallow: {path}" blocks them. A search engine renders the page before it judges it, and a page without its assets looks broken.
seo.imageBlock: Every crawler without its own rules is cut off from the images under this rule, because "Disallow: {path}" blocks them. An image search engine among them cannot show those images.
lint.legacyBadBots: This block list stops no crawler, because the {n} old scrapers and e-mail harvesters it names never obeyed robots.txt. Block them at the server if you need to.
fetch.warn.serverError: Google stops crawling the whole site while this lasts, because robots.txt answered {status} and Google treats a server error as "block everything".
fetch.warn.rateLimited: Google stops crawling the whole site while this lasts, because robots.txt answered 429 Too Many Requests and Google treats that like a server error.
fetch.warn.forbidden: Crawlers read every page and follow none of your rules, because robots.txt answered {status} and they treat that as "no restrictions".
fetch.warn.contentType: Crawlers may ignore the whole file, because it is served as {type}. Serve it as text/plain.
fetch.warn.contentTypeMissing: Crawlers may ignore the whole file, because it is served without a Content-Type header. Serve it as text/plain.
fetch.warn.htmlBody: Crawlers find no rules and read every page, because /robots.txt serves an HTML page with status 200. They treat that like a missing robots.txt.
security.category.version.label: Version disclosure
security.category.version.advice: These files name the software and its version, which is what an attacker looks up first. Delete them from the server instead of hiding them here.
security.category.maintenance.label: Maintenance scripts
security.category.maintenance.advice: Installers and update scripts must not be reachable after setup. Remove them, or restrict them by IP address.
security.category.server.label: Server internals
security.category.server.advice: These paths belong to the server, not the site. If nothing runs there, remove the rule; it only points at them.
security.reason.versionFile: File that names the software version
security.reason.licenseFile: Licence file that identifies the software
security.reason.xmlrpc: XML-RPC endpoint, a common brute-force target
security.reason.dependencies: Dependency directory that reveals the libraries in use
security.reason.platformDefault: Default path of {platform}, published by every site on it

sales.title: Now keep it that way
sales.body: A robots.txt changes with a deploy, a plugin upgrade or a theme edit. One line can cut a site out of Google or hand every AI crawler the whole archive. You have the picture for today; these are the three ways to keep it.
sales.free.title: Free account, free forever
sales.free.body: Watch one domain and get told when its robots.txt changes. No card, no trial that expires, no call with anyone.
sales.free.f2: An email when the file changes, with what it does to each crawler
sales.free.f3: The full report and its history, kept
sales.free.note: Email and a password, or Google. Nothing else is asked.
sales.self.title: Or do it yourself
sales.self.body: The engine is a command, a GitHub Action and a package. Same checks as this page, running on your machine or in your pipeline, failing the build when the file breaks.
sales.self.claude: Claude can run it for you: install the command and ask it to audit a domain, or wire the Action into your repository.
sales.watch.title: Or have us watch the market
sales.watch.body: Your domains and your competitors', checked as often as every quarter of an hour, with the alert going wherever your team already reads.
sales.watch.f1: Competitors side by side, per crawler
sales.watch.f2: Slack, Teams, SMS, webhook, on call
sales.watch.f3: Reports you can send to a client
sales.after.errors: The errors above are in force now, in the first file a crawler reads. Each one is listed with its fix. What this page cannot show you is the next change, which usually arrives with a deploy.
sales.after.training: Every AI crawler above is allowed to read this site. If nobody decided that, nobody will notice when it changes.
sales.after.warnings: Nothing here is broken today, but the warnings above are how it starts. A robots.txt gets worse one line at a time, and nobody reads it between deploys.
sales.after.clean: This file is in good order today. The next deploy, plugin upgrade or theme edit is the one to worry about, and watching it is what that takes.
ui.export.locked.note: These exports live in your account, which is free forever and takes an email and a password. The report on this page stays free and whole either way.

ui.consent.body: We would like to count visits with Google Analytics, which sets cookies in your browser and sends Google the page you are on. It is not needed to check a robots.txt, so it is your choice, and the check works exactly the same either way.
ui.consent.never: The address you check is never sent to Google, whichever you choose.
